We show that the globular cluster mass function (GCMF) in the Milky Way depends on cluster half-mass density (rho_h) in the sense that the turnover mass M_TO increases with rho_h while the width of the GCMF decreases. We argue that this is the expected signature of the slow erosion of a mass function that initially rose towards low masses, predominantly through cluster evaporation driven by internal two-body relaxation. We find excellent agreement between the observed GCMF -- including its dependence on internal density rho_h, central concentration c, and Galactocentric distance r_gc -- and a simple model in which the relaxation-driven mass-loss rates of clusters are approximated by -dM/dt = mu_ev ~ rho_h^{1/2}. In particular, we recover the well-known insensitivity of M_TO to r_gc. This feature does not derive from a literal ``universality'' of the GCMF turnover mass, but rather from a significant variation of M_TO with rho_h -- the expected outcome of relaxation-driven cluster disruption -- plus significant scatter in rho_h as a function of r_gc. Our conclusions are the same if the evaporation rates are assumed to depend instead on the mean volume or surface densities of clusters inside their tidal radii, as mu_ev ~ rho_t^{1/2} or mu_ev ~ Sigma_t^{3/4} -- alternative prescriptions that are physically motivated but involve cluster properties (rho_t and Sigma_t) that are not as well defined or as readily observable as rho_h. In all cases, the normalization of mu_ev required to fit the GCMF implies cluster lifetimes that are within the range of standard values (although falling towards the low end of this range). Our analysis does not depend on any assumptions or information about velocity anisotropy in the globular cluster system.

# The Density Dependence of the Milky Way's Globular Cluster Mass Function

## Observational Evidence

The globular cluster mass function of the Milky Way exhibits a systematic dependence on the internal structural properties of its constituent clusters. Specifically, when clusters are examined as a function of their half-mass density, two clear trends emerge: the turnover mass—the characteristic mass at which the peak of the mass function occurs—increases with increasing cluster half-mass density, while simultaneously the width of the mass function decreases. This coupled behavior reveals that denser clusters are, on average, both more massive at their turnover and more narrowly distributed in mass.

## Physical Interpretation

This density dependence is precisely the signature one would expect from the slow, sustained erosion of an initially low-mass-rising mass function. As clusters age, they steadily lose mass, and the accumulated effect of this erosion sculpts the shape of the present-day mass function. The dominant driver of this process is cluster evaporation arising from internal two-body relaxation, whereby gravitational encounters between individual stars gradually populate the high-velocity tail of the stellar distribution, allowing stars to escape the cluster's potential over time. Because the rate of this relaxation-driven mass loss depends on internal density, clusters of differing densities experience different degrees of erosion, naturally producing the observed correlations.

## A Simple Predictive Model

The physical picture can be quantified with a straightforward model in which the relaxation-driven mass-loss rate is approximated by a dependence on the half-mass density of the form −dM/dt ∝ ρₕ^(1/2). Despite its simplicity, this prescription closely reproduces the observed mass function. Crucially, it also captures the way the mass function varies with several independent cluster properties, including internal density, central concentration, and Galactocentric distance. The model's ability to match all of these dependencies simultaneously provides strong support for the interpretation that internal relaxation, rather than some external or universal process, governs the evolution of the mass function.

## Resolving the Galactocentric Distance Puzzle

A long-standing observation is that the turnover mass of the globular cluster mass function appears remarkably insensitive to Galactocentric distance, a fact often invoked as evidence for a universal turnover mass established at cluster formation. The present framework offers a different and more natural explanation. The turnover mass is not, in fact, universal; rather, it varies systematically with internal density. The apparent constancy with Galactocentric distance arises because there is substantial scatter in the relationship between cluster density and distance. This scatter effectively washes out the underlying density dependence when clusters are binned by distance alone, giving the misleading impression of a distance-independent turnover mass.

## Robustness of the Conclusions

The principal conclusions do not hinge on the specific form chosen for the mass-loss prescription. Alternative formulations, such as those based on tidal volume densities or surface densities, lead to the same qualitative and quantitative results. Furthermore, in all of these cases, the inferred cluster lifetimes fall within the range of standard values, and these results are obtained without invoking any special assumptions about the velocity anisotropy of the stellar orbits. This robustness reinforces the conclusion that internal two-body relaxation is the fundamental process shaping the Milky Way's globular cluster mass function.

# The Density Dependence of the Milky Way Globular Cluster Mass Function

## Introduction

The globular cluster mass function (GCMF) of the Milky Way exhibits a characteristic form that has long attracted theoretical attention. When expressed as the number of clusters per unit mass, the distribution peaks at a well-defined "turnover" mass of roughly 2 × 10⁵ solar masses, declining toward both higher and lower masses. Understanding the physical origin of this shape—and particularly the near-constancy of the turnover mass across the Galaxy—remains a central problem in the study of star cluster populations and their dynamical evolution.

This study investigates how the shape of the GCMF depends on the half-mass density of individual clusters. Rather than treating the observed mass function as a fixed initial condition, we model it as the outcome of a slow, ongoing erosion process. The fundamental premise is that clusters are born with a mass function that rises toward low masses—consistent with the power-law distributions observed for young cluster populations—and that this initial function is gradually sculpted over billions of years by the preferential destruction of low-mass systems.

## The Model

The physical mechanism driving this evolution is relaxation-driven evaporation. Two-body relaxation causes stars to gradually diffuse to energies exceeding the escape velocity, allowing them to leave the cluster. Over time, this steady mass loss erodes clusters from below, systematically depleting the low-mass end of the distribution and transforming an initially low-mass-rising function into the peaked distribution observed today.

A key simplifying assumption of our approach is that the mass-loss rate of a cluster is approximately proportional to the square root of its half-mass density. This scaling captures the essential dependence of the evaporation rate on internal cluster structure, since the relaxation timescale—and hence the rate at which stars escape—is governed by the cluster's density. By adopting this density-dependent formulation, the model naturally links the dynamical erosion of each cluster to its physical properties, allowing the resulting GCMF to depend explicitly on half-mass density.

## Results

When applied to the Milky Way globular cluster system, the model demonstrates excellent agreement with observations. Most notably, it reproduces the empirical finding that the turnover mass of the GCMF is remarkably insensitive to Galactocentric distance—clusters at widely different distances from the Galactic center share nearly the same characteristic mass at the peak of their distribution.

Crucially, our model reveals that this apparent universality is not fundamental. Instead, the near-constancy of the turnover mass emerges from the interplay between the variation of cluster density with Galactocentric position and the intrinsic scatter in cluster properties. In other words, the observed constancy is an emergent statistical outcome rather than evidence for a truly universal turnover mass. This reframing is significant, because it explains a long-puzzling regularity as a natural consequence of density-dependent evaporation rather than requiring special initial conditions or a fine-tuned physical scale.

Furthermore, the cluster lifetimes implied by the model are consistent with standard values derived from independent dynamical considerations. This internal consistency reinforces the physical plausibility of the framework: the timescales required to erode the initial mass function into its present form align with our established understanding of how quickly clusters evaporate.

## Conclusions

Taken together, these results provide a physically grounded explanation for the structure of the Milky Way GCMF. By modeling the mass function as the product of slow, relaxation-driven erosion with a mass-loss rate scaling as the square root of density, we account for the observed shape of the distribution and the apparent invariance of its turnover mass without invoking assumptions about velocity anisotropy in the cluster system. This represents an important simplification relative to earlier models, which often relied on specific anisotropy prescriptions to reproduce the observed features. Our findings suggest that the density dependence of cluster evaporation is the primary driver shaping the GCMF, offering a coherent and dynamically motivated picture of how the globular cluster population has evolved over the lifetime of the Galaxy.

# The Globular Cluster Mass Function in the Milky Way

The **Globular Cluster Mass Function (GCMF)** is one of the most important tools astronomers use to understand the population of star clusters that orbit our galaxy. In simple terms, the GCMF describes how the total number of globular clusters is distributed across different masses—that is, how many low-mass, intermediate-mass, and high-mass clusters exist within a galaxy such as the **Milky Way**.

## What Are Globular Clusters?

Globular clusters are dense, roughly spherical collections of hundreds of thousands to millions of stars, bound together by gravity. The Milky Way hosts roughly 150 known globular clusters, most of which are extremely old—often more than 10 billion years. Because they formed during the earliest epochs of the galaxy's history, these clusters serve as valuable "fossils" that record the conditions of the early universe.

## The Shape of the GCMF

A striking feature of the GCMF in the Milky Way is that it is not a simple power law. Instead, when plotted, it typically takes on a characteristic **peaked, log-normal shape**. This means:

- There is a **turnover mass** near which the greatest number of clusters is found, usually around a few times 10⁵ solar masses.
- The number of clusters declines on both the low-mass and high-mass sides of this peak.

This log-normal distribution appears remarkably consistent not only in the Milky Way but also across many other galaxies, making the peak of the GCMF a useful "standard candle" for estimating cosmic distances.

## Why the GCMF Matters

The shape of the GCMF holds clues about how globular clusters form and, more importantly, how they are **destroyed over time**. Astronomers believe that clusters were originally born with a different, likely power-law mass distribution. Over billions of years, several processes gradually reshaped this distribution:

- **Two-body relaxation**, which causes stars to slowly escape from clusters.
- **Tidal disruption** from the gravitational pull of the Milky Way.
- **Dynamical friction**, which drags massive clusters toward the galactic center.

These effects preferentially destroy low-mass clusters, carving the original distribution into the peaked GCMF we observe today.

## Conclusion

The Globular Cluster Mass Function is far more than a statistical curve—it is a window into the formation and evolution of the Milky Way. By studying the GCMF, astronomers can reconstruct the dynamical history of our galaxy, test theories of cluster destruction, and even measure distances across the universe. As observational surveys grow more detailed, the GCMF will continue to refine our understanding of how galaxies like the Milky Way assembled and evolved over cosmic time.

# Abstract

The mass function of globular clusters (GCs) encodes the integrated history of dynamical evolution and destruction processes that have shaped these systems over a Hubble time. We investigate how the present-day mass function of Milky Way globular clusters depends on cluster half-mass density and explore the physical connection to two-body relaxation-driven evaporation. Using a sample of Galactic GCs with well-determined structural parameters and masses, we divide clusters into bins of half-mass density and examine the resulting mass distributions. We find that the low-mass end of the mass function exhibits a systematic dependence on half-mass density: high-density clusters display a pronounced depletion of low-mass systems, whereas low-density clusters retain a shallower mass function extending to lower masses. This trend is consistent with the theoretical expectation that the mass-loss rate driven by relaxation and subsequent evaporation across the tidal boundary scales with the internal relaxation timescale, which is itself a function of cluster density. We show that clusters with shorter relaxation times—corresponding to higher half-mass densities—lose mass more rapidly and are preferentially destroyed or driven toward dissolution, thereby carving the observed density-dependent turnover in the mass function. We compare our results to predictions from analytic evaporation models and N-body simulations, finding broad agreement with a picture in which the mass function evolves from a power-law or Schechter-like initial distribution toward the observed peaked distribution through density-dependent dynamical erosion. These findings reinforce the role of internal relaxation as a primary driver of globular cluster mass evolution and provide observational constraints on the timescales governing cluster disruption in the Galactic environment. We discuss implications for the initial cluster mass function and for connecting Milky Way GCs to their formation conditions in the early universe.

# Abstract

**The Dependence of Globular Cluster Mass Function Evolution on Host Galaxy Environment**

We present a systematic investigation of the globular cluster mass function (GCMF) and its dependence on the local mass density of the host galactic environment, parameterized by the halo density ρ_h. Using a combination of numerical N-body simulations and semi-analytic modeling of cluster dynamical evolution, we track the long-term erosion of the initial cluster mass function under the combined effects of two-body relaxation, tidal stripping, and dynamical friction across a range of environmental densities.

Our principal result is that the characteristic turnover mass, M_TO, of the evolved GCMF increases systematically with increasing ρ_h. This trend reflects the enhanced efficiency of cluster disruption in denser environments, where low-mass clusters are preferentially destroyed, shifting the peak of the surviving population toward higher masses. Concurrently, we find that the width (dispersion) of the GCMF decreases with increasing ρ_h, indicating a narrowing of the mass distribution as environmental processing more efficiently removes the low-mass tail and homogenizes the surviving cluster population.

We demonstrate that these coupled trends arise naturally from a tidally-driven mass-loss prescription in which the cluster dissolution rate scales as dM/dt ∝ ρ_h^(1/2). This scaling, consistent with the expected dependence of the tidal field strength on the local density, quantitatively reproduces both the upward migration of M_TO and the contraction of the GCMF width as functions of environment. The characteristic dissolution timescale correspondingly decreases as ρ_h^(-1/2), providing a unified framework linking the present-day GCMF morphology to the density structure of the host halo.

These findings suggest that the observed near-universality of the GCMF turnover mass may mask underlying environmental variations, and that careful accounting of ρ_h is essential for interpreting GCMF measurements as probes of cluster formation and destruction history. We discuss the implications of these results for the use of globular clusters as cosmological distance indicators and as tracers of galaxy assembly.

---

# Modeling the Milky Way Globular Cluster Mass Function through Relaxation-Driven Evaporation: Density Prescriptions and Cluster Longevity

## Abstract

The characteristic peaked shape of the Galactic globular cluster mass function (GCMF), with its turnover near ~2×10⁵ M☉, represents a fundamental constraint on theories of cluster evolution and destruction. We present a semi-analytic framework modeling the dynamical evolution of the Milky Way globular cluster system, with particular emphasis on two-body relaxation-driven evaporation as the dominant mass-loss mechanism sculpting the low-mass end of the distribution. Assuming a power-law initial cluster mass function consistent with young massive clusters observed in the local universe, we integrate individual cluster mass-loss histories over a Hubble time and evaluate the resulting present-day GCMF against observational data.

A central focus of this work concerns the sensitivity of predicted mass-loss rates to the adopted prescription relating the evaporation timescale to the local Galactic environment. We compare formulations in which the mass-loss rate scales with the mean host density traversed along the orbit against alternatives tied to the tidal field strength, angular velocity, and epicyclic frequency. We demonstrate that these prescriptions, while nearly degenerate for circular orbits in an isothermal halo, diverge substantially for eccentric orbits and in the inner Galaxy, producing measurable differences in the predicted turnover mass and the width of the evolved distribution.

Our results indicate that relaxation-driven evaporation, when combined with a realistic distribution of orbital parameters and accounting for the influence of stellar mass segregation and the depletion of the stellar mass function, naturally reproduces the observed near-universal turnover. However, we find that the inferred cluster lifetimes—and consequently the implied initial cluster population and its total mass—depend critically on whether mass loss is treated as constant or explicitly time-dependent as clusters dissolve. We discuss the implications of these findings for the fraction of the primordial cluster population that has survived to the present, the contribution of dissolved clusters to the Galactic stellar halo and bulge, and the reconciliation of dynamical models with cosmological simulations of cluster formation. We conclude that discriminating among density prescriptions requires joint modeling of the GCMF alongside the spatial and kinematic distribution of surviving clusters.

---

*Keywords:* globular clusters — stellar dynamics — two-body relaxation — galaxy evolution — mass function
